title: Asthma attack
blurb: Recognise an acute asthma attack, help the patient use salbutamol through a spacer, and know the signs that mean 999.
question: A patient with asthma starts coughing and wheezing while the dentist prepares a filling. She is leaning forward, can't finish a sentence without stopping for breath, and the muscles in her neck are working hard. What do you do first, and what tells you this attack is severe?

teach.body: In an asthma attack the airways narrow in three ways: the muscle around them tightens, the lining swells, and extra mucus is made. Air gets trapped, so the patient wheezes (mostly on breathing out), coughs and feels a tight chest. In the surgery, attacks can be set off by anxiety, cold air, exertion such as climbing stairs, allergens, or forgetting to use a regular inhaler. Ask every asthmatic patient to bring their reliever inhaler to each appointment.

bands.label: Moderate: wheeze, cough, talks in sentences
Severe: can't finish a sentence, neck muscles working, fast breathing
Life-threatening: silent chest, blue lips, exhausted or confused

teach.caption: A quiet chest in a patient who is struggling is not improvement: it means very little air is moving.

steps.label: Salbutamol via spacer
steps.sub: 1 puff every 30–60 seconds, up to 10 puffs

steps.label: Call 999
steps.sub: Severe or life-threatening, or no better

steps.label: Keep repeating salbutamol
steps.sub: While you wait for the ambulance

items.label: puffs maximum per round, then repeat as needed
large-volume, to get the dose into the lungs

teach.caption: Use the patient's own inhaler if they have it, or the practice emergency salbutamol. For children aged 2–17, the round can be repeated at 10–20 minute intervals.

teach.h: Why salbutamol, and why a spacer
teach.body: Salbutamol is a reliever: it relaxes the tightened airway muscle within minutes. A panicking, breathless patient struggles to press the inhaler and breathe in at the same moment, so much of the dose ends up on the back of the throat. A large-volume spacer holds the puff in a chamber so the patient can breathe it in over several normal breaths, and far more reaches the lungs. If there's no spacer, the inhaler can still be used on its own.

teach.caption: If a patient hands you two inhalers, the blue reliever is the one that helps now.

teach.text: Not every wheeze is asthma. Sudden wheeze with swollen lips or tongue, a rash or faintness after a trigger is anaphylaxis, and needs IM adrenaline. And never lay an asthmatic patient flat: breathing is easier sitting up.

teach.body: Call 999 if the patient shows any severe or life-threatening sign, if they don't improve with salbutamol, if they get worse, or if you're unsure. Keep giving salbutamol while you wait. Even a mild attack that settles fully means treatment stops for the day: the dentist decides on next steps, and the patient should be advised to have their asthma reviewed by their GP or asthma nurse.

items: Asthma attack: wheeze, cough, tight chest, breathlessness from narrowed airways.
Sit upright, reassure, use the blue salbutamol reliever.
Salbutamol 100 µg: 1 puff via large-volume spacer every 30–60 s, up to 10 puffs, repeat as needed.
Severe: can't finish sentences, neck muscles working. Life-threatening: silent chest, blue lips, exhaustion, confusion.
Severe, life-threatening or not improving: oxygen 15 L/min and call 999.

summary: You can now explain what narrows the airways in an asthma attack, grade an attack as moderate, severe or life-threatening, give salbutamol correctly through a spacer, and know when oxygen and a 999 call are needed.

A.q: A patient with asthma becomes wheezy and breathless during treatment but can still speak in sentences. What should you do first?
options: Lie her flat with her legs raised
Sit her upright, use her reliever
Give glucose gel on the gum
Give GTN spray under the tongue
A.why: Sitting upright makes breathing easier, and the blue salbutamol reliever relaxes the narrowed airways.

whyNot.0: Lying flat makes breathing harder for an asthmatic patient.
whyNot.2: Glucose treats hypoglycaemia, not narrowed airways.
whyNot.3: GTN treats angina and has no effect on asthma.

A.q: Which sign shows that an asthma attack is severe?
options: Coughing when the water spray is used
Asking for a glass of water
A.why: Being unable to complete a sentence in one breath is a recognised sign of a severe attack, along with neck muscle use and fast breathing.

whyNot.0: A cough from the water spray is a minor irritation, not a sign of severity.
whyNot.1: A mild wheeze with normal speech fits a moderate attack.
whyNot.2: Asking for water says nothing about how hard the patient is working to breathe.

A.q: How is the practice's emergency salbutamol given during an acute attack?
options: 2 puffs under the tongue every 5 min
1 puff via a spacer every 30–60 s
10 puffs into the mouth all at once
1 puff into the nose every 15 min
A.why: SDCEP advises 1 puff (100 micrograms) via a large-volume spacer every 30–60 seconds, up to 10 puffs, repeated as needed.

whyNot.0: Two puffs under the tongue is how GTN spray is given for angina.
whyNot.2: Puffs given all at once aren't breathed in properly; they're given one at a time.
whyNot.3: Salbutamol is breathed into the lungs, not sprayed into the nose.

B.q: Which sign suggests a life-threatening asthma attack?
options: A silent chest with blue lips
B.why: A silent chest means almost no air is moving, and blue lips (cyanosis) mean low oxygen: both are life-threatening signs.

whyNot.0: A loud wheeze shows air is still moving; it's worrying but not the most dangerous sign.
whyNot.1: Cough and chest tightness are typical of any asthma attack.
whyNot.3: Short phrases suggest a severe attack, but not the life-threatening features.

B.q: Why is a large-volume spacer used with the salbutamol inhaler in an emergency?
options: It turns a reliever into a preventer
It makes the dose last for 12 hours
More of the dose reaches the lungs
B.why: The spacer holds the puff so a breathless patient can inhale it over several breaths, so more reaches the lungs.

whyNot.0: A spacer doesn't change the drug; salbutamol is always a reliever.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol's effect lasts a few hours, and a spacer doesn't lengthen it.
whyNot.3: A spacer improves delivery but doesn't replace calling 999 when needed.

B.q: A wheezy patient hands you two inhalers, one blue and one brown. Which will help the attack?
B.why: The blue reliever (salbutamol) opens the airways within minutes. The brown preventer works over days and weeks.

whyNot.1: A steroid preventer reduces inflammation over time and won't relieve an acute attack.
whyNot.2: They work in different ways and at very different speeds.
whyNot.3: Oxygen helps in a severe attack, but salbutamol is the key treatment.

C.q: After 10 puffs of salbutamol, a patient still can't finish a sentence and is tiring. What should happen?
options: Wait 30 minutes to see if it settles
Send her home to rest in bed
C.why: A severe attack that isn't responding needs a 999 call, with salbutamol repeated (and oxygen given) while you wait.

whyNot.1: Waiting lets a severe attack become life-threatening.
whyNot.2: Sending a severely breathless patient home is unsafe.
whyNot.3: A preventer works too slowly to help an attack.

C.q: What is the best position for a patient having an asthma attack?
options: On her side in recovery position
C.why: Sitting upright and leaning slightly forward lets the breathing muscles work most easily.

whyNot.0: Lying back with legs raised is for a faint, and it makes breathing harder.
whyNot.1: The recovery position is for an unconscious patient who is breathing.
whyNot.3: Walking increases the body's demand for oxygen and risks collapse.

C.q: Which is NOT part of managing an acute asthma attack in the surgery?
C.why: Laying an asthmatic patient flat makes breathing harder; they should sit upright.

whyNot.0: Reassurance helps because anxiety makes breathlessness worse.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol via a spacer is the main treatment.
whyNot.3: Calling 999 is right when the attack doesn't improve.

reteach.title: Breathing through a straw
reteach.question: Try breathing out hard through a thin drinking straw. That's how an asthma attack feels. What makes the straw narrow, and what opens it again?

blocks.body: Imagine each airway as a straw wrapped in a band of muscle. In an attack the band squeezes, the inside of the straw swells and gets sticky with mucus. Air can get in but struggles to get out, so it whistles (wheeze). Salbutamol loosens the band, and the spacer makes sure the medicine actually reaches the straws rather than the back of the throat.

blocks.h: One question decides the next step

children.edge: Can't finish sentences or silent chest
children.label: Oxygen + call 999

explain.body: Three things narrow the airways: tightened muscle, a swollen lining and extra mucus. Trapped air whistles as the patient breathes out.

test.q: What causes the wheeze in an asthma attack?
test.why: Wheeze is the sound of air forced through narrowed airways in the lungs.

whyNot.0: Tongue swelling is a sign of anaphylaxis.
whyNot.2: Fluid around the heart is unrelated to asthma.
whyNot.3: A blocked nose doesn't cause wheeze from the chest.

explain.body: Moderate: wheeze, but full sentences. Severe: can't finish a sentence in one breath, neck and shoulder muscles working, fast breathing. Life-threatening: silent chest, blue lips, exhaustion, confusion.

test.q: A patient's wheeze has gone quiet, but she is drowsy and her lips look blue. What does this mean?
test.why: A silent chest with blue lips and drowsiness means very little air is moving: a life-threatening attack.

whyNot.0: The wheeze has stopped because so little air is moving, not because she is better.
whyNot.1: Drowsiness here is a sign of exhaustion and low oxygen.
whyNot.2: A preventer works too slowly; she needs emergency help now.

explain.body: One puff (100 micrograms) through a large-volume spacer every 30 to 60 seconds, up to 10 puffs, then repeat as needed. The spacer lets the patient breathe the dose in over several breaths.

test.q: What is the maximum number of salbutamol puffs in one round before repeating?
test.why: SDCEP advises up to 10 puffs, one every 30–60 seconds, repeated as needed.

whyNot.0: Two puffs is the GTN dose for angina, and too little for an attack.
whyNot.1: Four puffs is below the recommended maximum for a round.
whyNot.3: Twenty puffs is not the recommended round.

explain.body: Call 999 for any severe or life-threatening sign, or if salbutamol isn't working. Give oxygen at 15 L/min and keep giving salbutamol. If wheeze comes with swelling or rash after a trigger, think anaphylaxis.

test.q: A patient becomes wheezy with swollen lips and a rash straight after an antibiotic. Which drug is needed first?
test.why: Wheeze with swelling and rash after a trigger is anaphylaxis, and IM adrenaline is the first-line drug.

whyNot.0: Salbutamol helps wheeze but doesn't treat the whole allergic reaction.
whyNot.3: Aspirin is for suspected heart attack and could itself trigger allergy.
